title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmarking Playbook
author: Emily Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling guidance, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes highlights, known issues, and primary runbooks used by the serving/runtime team. It is intended as the canonical on-call and engineering reference for making changes that affect latency, throughput, and memory safety for inference workloads.

Scope and audience
- Audience: runtime engineers, infra engineers, performance SREs, and platform product managers.
- Scope: production GPU/CPU inference stacks used by Redwood Hosted and Dedicated deployments; excludes private deployment packaging steps (see eng-private-deployments).

1) High-level runtime architecture

Short summary
The serving runtime is a modular, GPU-optimized inference engine with three primary layers: request ingress and routing, execution runtime (kernel selection + KV cache + batching), and storage/telemetry. Routing is policy-driven (latency/cost/region) and the runtime supports model variants (FP16, quantized int8/4, and optimiser-specific kernels).

Components and responsibilities
- Frontend/API gateway: auth, rate-limit, request shaping, and per-route quotas.
- Router & policy engine: selects target model variant, region, and fallback chain.
- Scheduling & batcher: maintains worker pools, continuous batching queues, and KV cache hot-paths.
- Execution engine: selects kernels, manages KV cache lifecycle, handles past-key-value tensors and attention mechanics.
- Metrics & tracing: token-level latency, GPU utilization, memory high-water marks, kernel-level timings.

SLOs and common thresholds
- P99 token latency (hosted-small models): <= 120ms per token.
- P95 tail for large context (>=8k tokens): <= 450ms per token.
- GPU memory headroom: reserve 5% of device memory for transient peaks.
- Error rate SLO: 0.1% request error rate monthly.

Ownership and escalation
- Runtime Team: primary owner for kernel selection, batching, and release coordination.
- Eng-SRE: owner for capacity planning and on-call escalation.
- Related on-call runbooks: see section 7.

2) Kernel selection and scheduling principles

Design goals
- Minimize end-to-end latency for latency-sensitive routes.
- Maximise throughput for batch-oriented, background workloads.
- Keep memory usage predictable across model variants and quantization profiles.

Kernel selection logic (decision flow)
1. Determine model architecture and preferred kernel family (e.g., FlashAttention vX for decoder-only transformers).
2. Inspect request context length and past-key-value hit ratio. If high PKV reuse, select kernel path optimized for KV streaming.
3. Evaluate quantization profile: if int8 quantized variant exists and model passes quality gates, prefer quantized kernel for throughput/cost unless latency SLO demands FP16.
4. Verify hardware capability (compute capability, TensorCore availability). Fallback to CPU CUDA kernels only if GPU unavailable.

Scheduling knobs and their defaults
- worker_pool.size: dynamic (default = GPU_count * 2).
- batcher.max_batch_size: 64 for large models, 256 for embeddings workers.
- batcher.max_latency_ms: 8ms for low-latency routes, 50-100ms for throughput-oriented jobs.
- prefetch_kv_window: 2 (number of next-request frames to prefetch into KV cache).

Best practices
- For low-latency interactive routes, set max_latency_ms <= 10ms and reduce max_batch_size.
- For background/bulk transforms (embeddings or batch generation), increase max_batch_size and max_latency_ms to improve GPU utilization.
- Pin scheduled jobs to specific GPU-memory classes to reduce noisy neighbor effects.

3) Profiling playbook (how to diagnose perf issues)

When to profile
- P99 latency increases > 20% over baseline.
- New model variant rollout with unexplained cost regressions.
- GPU memory OOMs, or elevated swap activity.

Quick triage checklist
1. Reproduce on staging with same request shape (prompt length, batch sizes, sampling parameters).
2. Capture telemetry window: 2 minutes pre-incident, 2 minutes post-incident. Use run_profile.sh (see CLI).
3. Check kernel-level timings and kernel queue depth (NVIDIA Nsight metrics or ROCm equivalents).

Tools and commands
- run_profile.sh: utilities/runtime/profile/run_profile.sh --model <model> --duration 120 --sample-rate 1
- nvidia-smi dmon / nvidia-smi topo -m for NVLink checks.
- collect_kernels.py: aggregates per-kernel durations from runtime tracing logs.
- perf trace example: sudo perf record -g -e cycles:u -p <pid> -- sleep 30

Interpreting outputs
- If kernel execution time dominates (90%+ of token latency): focus on kernel selection and quantization profile.
- If scheduling/queueing dominates: inspect batcher queue lengths and batcher.max_latency_ms setting.
- If memcpy or PCIe stalls appear: check model sharding and placement; consider model sharding across multiple GPUs or use NVLink-enabled machines.

4) Benchmarking suite and methodology

Principles
- Benchmarks must be reproducible, parameterized by model, sequence length, temperature, and routing policy.
- Use representative production traffic shapes stored in prompt-sets-and-benchmarks.
- Report both latency percentiles and token/second throughput under steady-state.

Standard benchmark jobs (CI and gated checks)
- smoke-latency: single-client, interactive profile for common prompt shapes.
- throughput-batch: multi-client concurrent request generator for throughput; key metric: tokens/sec.
- cold-start: measure first-token latency with empty KV cache.
- pkv-hot: workload where PKV hit-rate >= 80% to validate caching benefits.

Example YAML job config
| field | example | notes |
|---|---|---|
| model | gptx-6B-fp16 | model family used |
| seq_len | 1024 | sequence length for the run |
| clients | 32 | concurrent clients |
| batcher.max_batch_size | 64 | runtime config override |
| duration | 600s | run duration |

Running a benchmark (CLI)
1. checkout infra/benchmarks and set BENCHMARK_TARGET env.
2. ./bin/run_benchmark --config=bench_configs/gptx-6b-throughput.yaml --report-dir=/tmp/reports/`date +%s`
3. Upload report: ./bin/upload_benchmark --dir /tmp/reports/<id>

Reporting format
- CSV summary line: timestamp, model, seq_len, clients, p50_token_ms, p95_token_ms, p99_token_ms, tokens_per_sec, gpu_util
- JSON full report: produced by bench-aggregator. Stored under s3://rwd-bench-reports/<date>/<id>.

5) Release notes (runtime releases and what to check)

Release checklist for runtime rollouts
1. Ensure all kernels built against target CUDA/ROCm versions.
2. Run smoke-latency and throughput-batch on staging with the same fleet size.
3. Verify rollout can be rolled back via route-level model-variant fallback.
4. Confirm telemetry dashboards reflect new metric names if changed.
5. Notify Eng-SRE and on-call 24h before broad rollout.

Recent notable changes (high level)
- 2026-05-10: Added FlashAttention v3 kernels; observed 12-20% token-latency reduction for decoder models in staging.
- 2026-06-02: Introduced dynamic prefetch_kv_window and pretrain profiling hooks.
- 2026-07-01: Default batcher.max_latency_ms reduced from 20ms -> 8ms for public low-latency routes.

6) Known issues (active and mitigations)

Active issues summary (as of last_updated)
- Issue: intermittent OOMs on A100-40GB for long-context (>=16k) streams.
  - Symptoms: OOM logs, partial token generations then error 500.
  - Mitigation: reduce max_sequence_length to 12k or use sharded model placement. Schedule target: implement streaming KV eviction by 2026-09-01.
- Issue: Slight accuracy regression for int8 quantized variant on code-generation prompts.
  - Symptoms: failing unit tests in eval harness for specific prompt set.
  - Mitigation: route codegen workloads to FP16 by default; add quantization calibration for codegen models.
- Issue: NVLink topology mismatch leads to thrash on multi-GPU shards.
  - Mitigation: pin shards to NVLink-connected pairs, update placement hints in scheduler.

How to file a new known issue
1. Create an issue in Jira project RUNTIME with label "known-issue".
2. Add reproduction steps and attach profiler outputs.
3. Assign a POC and add to the next weekly runtime triage.

7) Runbooks (operational procedures)

A. High-latency incident runbook (shortened)
1. Acknowledge alert and capture window_id.
2. Identify impacted routes/models: query /observability/latency by route in last 5m.
3. If P99 increase > 2x baseline, switch affected route to fallback variant via router UI (fallback -> fp16/quant).
4. If GPU queueing observed, temporarily reduce worker_pool.size on that host and increase batcher.max_latency_ms for throughput routes.
5. If OOM, follow OOM runbook (B).

B. GPU OOM runbook
1. Identify host and model shard from OOM logs.
2. Execute emergency action: remove non-critical shards from the GPU and update placement.
3. If persistent, drain host via autoscaler and re-balance shards.
4. Postmortem: annotate incident with kernel-level memory peak and model config.

C. Release rollback procedure
1. Trigger route-level model variant rollback from router console.
2. Monitor p50/p95/p99 and error rate for 30 minutes.
3. If rollback fails, scale down affected service and engage infra lead for emergency rollback.

Runbook ownership and contact list
- Runtime Pager: rotation (see eng-sre/runbooks)
- Escalation: <oncall_phone> (Eng-SRE lead), <infra_slack_channel>

8) Team wiki and knowledge sharing

Where to find more detailed artifacts
- Kernel performance traces: s3://rwd-traces/serving/runtime/<date>/
- Benchmark reports: s3://rwd-bench-reports/<date>/
- Prompt sets and evals: confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks

Recommended onboarding checklist for new runtime engineers
1. Read this doc and run the bench harness locally against a small model.
2. Shadow on-call for two weeks and run at least one post-incident write-up.
3. Contribute one benchmark or profiling script to infra/benchmarks.

Appendices

Appendix A: Example config snippets
- Example runtime flags (YAML):
  runtime_flags:
    worker_pool_size: 8
    batcher:
      max_batch_size: 64
      max_latency_ms: 8
    prefetch_kv_window: 2

Appendix B: CLI/Tooling references
- run_profile.sh and collect_kernels.py live in repo: infra/tools/runtime-profiling.
- Bench harness: infra/benchmarks. See README in that folder for setup.

Appendix C: Glossary
- PKV: past-key-value cache used for autoregressive decoding.
- Kernel family: group of optimized GPU kernels (e.g., FlashAttention, Triton custom kernels).
